description:
Red Osier Dogwood (Cornus sericea) A.k.a. American Dogwood. Large, native shrub that grows 1.5–4 meters tall in wet ground, along banks of rivers, creeks, ponds, and marshes. Twigs are purplish-red, strigose or villous. Leaves elliptic to ovate or lanceolate, bases obtuse or rounded, secondary veins 4–7 on each side of blade, prominent beneath, surfaces abaxially pubescent, adaxially strigose, Petioles 6–30 mm. Inflorescences flat-topped with many-branched cymes, strigose or villous, hairs. Flower corollas white to cream. Fruits ellipsoidal, 7–9 mm, white, seldom bluish. Peak bloom time: May–September. There are several subspecies.

Old Keiser farm corn field behind fen visible (I forget the new owner's name).

Band of red in center is regrowth of tilled dogwood about four years old in the riparian area of the south end of Hummocky Lick (creek) where it enters Honey Creek. 

This fen has been tilled twice in the past decade in an apparent attempt to alter the flow of water for farming.    Plus water is being directed from the east side of fen into Hummocky Lick (Livingston Drain #7) on the west side of fen.  This part of the fen has a hard trail running through it for power company service trucks that impedes the flow of water so what is being done to increase the rate of flow may only be normalizing the flow to what it was before the service trail was built. 

Observation:  All indications seem to suggest the first till killed off the small community of Yellow Lady's Slippers that used to grow in this area of the Hummocky Lick fen system (behind the old Keiser farm) on Kelly Rd.  This is the only place I've seen them in this tiny headwater to Honey Creek.

description:
Most of the plants around this time are just waking up from winter, so this Dwarf dogwood looks a little sad. It thrives in mostly well-draining soils of forests and forest edges and can mostly be found near stumps or fallen logs but can generally survive almost anywhere. Dwarf dogwood (Cornus Canadensis) is a low-hanging plant that can grow to about 4-9 inches in height and has one small pair of unique venation leaves (Alaska.org contributors). It goes by many different names, including bunchberry dogwood, bunchberry, dwarf dogwood, etc. 

The white bracts (which are not pictured here) are not flowers but specialized leaves that wait to release pollen through insects as they are attracted to the white leaves (Conlon). The bracts bloom around may to early July and produces the fruit in late summer. It is abundant in Alaska and many other northern states in the US and Canada. It is a widespread and easy plant to identify due to its leaf pattern, shape, bract color, and berries. (Stensvold) 

It produces a red edible berry called bunchberries because they grow in bunches but do not have a particularly good taste. Its texture is comparable to a cotton texture and has a singular seed (Stensvold). The flavor of the berries can be compared to a mild apple and are high in pectin, and can help thicken jams and jellies due to their abundance. It is also a vital foraging plant for ungulates like deer's and moose. (Conlon)

Work cited

description: Silky Dogwood (Kinnikinnik) - Cornus amomum (Swida amomum) Location: Durham NC (USA) Series for documenting ID of this shrubby dogwood. The other shrubby opposite-leaved dogwood in my area is Cornus foemina (=Swida foemina, sometimes listed as C./S. stricta). Keying these two definitively is a bit challenging, but here I have a detail photo of the 2nd and 3rd year twigs showing the brown pith characteristic of amomum (Cook, Radford). Weakley differentiates those two based on veins 5 or more per leaf side (amomum and others) vs. veins usually 3-4 per leaf side (foemina, etc). Weakley also differentiates amomum from the rather similar obliqua (not known from North Carolina) based on details of trichomes on underside of the leaves, as well as leaf shape. This specimen is consistent with amomum. References - Cook, Will, Trees, Shrubs, and Woody Vines of North Carolina (2015): www.carolinanature.com/trees/coam2.html - Flora of North America: www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=2... - Foote and Jones, Native Shrubs and Woody Vines of the Southeast (Timber Press, 1989), p. 101, plate 36 - Newcomb and Morrison, Newcomb's Wildflower Guide (Little, Brown; 1977), pp. 166-7 - Radford et al., Manual of the Vascular Flora of the Carolinas (UNC Press, 1968), pp. 790-792 - Weakley, Flora of the Southern United States (UNC Herbarium, 2020) p. 1129
